title: Agents & multi-step workflows
summary: Build agents that loop — calling tools, reading results, and deciding the next step until a multi-step task is done.
objectives: Explain what an LLM agent is and how it differs from a single prompt
Define tools the model can call, with names, descriptions, and input schemas
Run the agentic loop: call, read tool_use, execute, feed results back
Use the Anthropic tool runner to handle the loop for you
Decide when a simple workflow beats a full agent
Add guardrails: step limits, error handling, and human approval for risky actions

quiz.q: What makes an agent different from a single LLM call?
options: It loops — calling tools and deciding the next step until done
quiz.why: An agent runs a loop: the model picks an action (often a tool), you run it, feed the result back, and it decides what to do next.

quiz.q: When Claude wants to call a tool, what is the stop_reason on the response?
quiz.why: stop_reason becomes "tool_use". You execute the tool, return a tool_result, and call the API again to continue.

quiz.q: In a tool definition, what does input_schema describe?
options: The JSON shape of the arguments the tool expects
quiz.why: input_schema is JSON Schema describing the tool's parameters, so the model knows exactly what arguments to supply.

quiz.q: Why prefer a fixed workflow over an open-ended agent when you can?
quiz.answer: A workflow is more predictable, cheaper, faster, and easier to debug; reach for an agent only when the path can't be fully specified in advance.
quiz.why: Agents add cost and latency and are harder to reason about. Use the simplest tier that solves the task.

quiz.q: Name one guardrail you should add to an agentic loop.
quiz.answer: A maximum step (iteration) limit, error handling on tool calls, or human approval before irreversible actions.
quiz.why: Without limits an agent can loop forever or take harmful actions; bounds and approval gates keep it safe.

body_markdown:
## What is an agent?

Up to now you've sent one prompt and read one reply. An **agent** does more: it runs a **loop**. The model decides on an action — usually calling a **tool** — you run that action, hand the result back, and the model decides what to do next. It keeps going until the task is finished.

Think of it like long division. You don't solve it in one step; you repeat *estimate, multiply, subtract, bring down* until there's nothing left. An agent repeats *think, act, observe* the same way.

## Tools: giving the model hands

A **tool** is a function the model is allowed to call. You describe it with a name, a plain-English description, and an `input_schema` (JSON Schema) for its arguments. The model never runs your code — it just *asks* to, and your program does the running.

```python
tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"]
    }
}]
```

## The agentic loop

When the model wants a tool, the response comes back with `stop_reason == "tool_use"`. You execute the tool, append a `tool_result`, and call the API again. Repeat until `stop_reason == "end_turn"`.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Lagos?"}]
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for b in resp.content:
        if b.type == "tool_use":
            out = run_tool(b.name, b.input)   # your code
            results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": out})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
```

## Let the SDK run the loop

Writing that loop by hand is good for understanding. In practice the SDK's **tool runner** does it for you — you define tools as typed functions and iterate the results.

## Workflow vs agent

Not everything needs an agent. If you can write the steps down in advance — *extract, then summarise, then email* — that's a **workflow**, and a workflow is cheaper, faster, and far easier to debug. Reach for a full agent only when the path genuinely can't be planned ahead.

## Guardrails

An unbounded loop can spin forever or do something irreversible. Always add a **step limit**, handle tool errors gracefully, and require **human approval** before risky actions like sending money or deleting data.

## Your task

Build a tiny two-tool agent (e.g. a calculator and a search stub) and watch the loop call them in turn.

slides.title: Agents & multi-step workflows
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Four, where we build real portfolio projects. In this lesson we move beyond single prompts and learn how to build agents: programs that let the model loop, call tools, read the results, and decide what to do next. By the end you'll understand the agentic loop, how to define tools, and crucially, when an agent is the right choice and when a simpler workflow wins.

slides.title: What is an agent?
bullets: An agent runs a loop instead.
Stops when the task is done.
slides.narration: So far you've sent one prompt and read one reply. An agent does more than that: it runs a loop. The model decides on an action, your program carries it out, the result goes back, and the model decides the next step. It's a lot like long division, where you repeat the same little cycle until there's nothing left to do. The agent repeats think, act, observe.

slides.title: Tools give the model hands
bullets: A tool is a function the model may call.
You give a name, description, and schema.
The model asks; your code runs it.
slides.narration: On its own, a model can only produce text. Tools give it hands. A tool is just a function you let the model call. You describe it with a name, a plain English description, and an input schema written in Jason schema, which tells the model exactly what arguments to send. The important thing: the model never runs your code. It only asks to, and your program does the actual running.

slides.title: The agentic loop
bullets: You run the tool, return a result.
Call the A P I again to continue.
slides.narration: Here's the heart of it. When the model wants a tool, the response comes back with stop reason equal to tool use. You run the tool, append a tool result, and call the A P I again so the model can continue with what it learned. You keep looping until the stop reason is end turn, which means the model is finished. That loop is the whole idea of an agent.

slides.title: Feeding results back
bullets: Send results as a user message.
slides.narration: When you send results back, two details matter. First, append the assistant's message including its tool use blocks, so the conversation stays consistent. Second, every tool result must carry the matching tool use I D, so the model knows which call it answers. You bundle the results into a user message and send them on. Get the I D wrong and the request will fail.

slides.title: Let the SDK run the loop
bullets: The tool runner loops for you.
slides.code:
runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
  model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
  max_tokens=1024, tools=[get_weather],
  messages=msgs)
for message in runner:
    print(message)
slides.narration: Writing the loop by hand is great for understanding what's happening under the hood. But in real projects, the S D K's tool runner does it for you. You define your tools as typed Python functions, hand them over, and iterate the runner. It calls the model, runs your tools, feeds the results back, and stops when the model is done. Less boilerplate means fewer bugs.

slides.title: Workflow vs agent
bullets: Can you list the steps ahead of time?
Workflows are cheaper and easier to debug.
Use an agent only when the path is open-ended.
slides.narration: Here's a judgement call that separates beginners from professionals. Not everything needs an agent. If you can write the steps down in advance, like extract, then summarise, then email, that's a workflow, and a workflow is cheaper, faster, and far easier to debug. Reach for a full agent only when the path genuinely can't be planned ahead, because the task is open ended and the model must decide its own route.

slides.title: Guardrails
slides.narration: An unbounded loop can spin forever or do something you can't undo. So always add guardrails. Put a hard limit on the number of steps. Handle tool errors so one failure doesn't crash everything. And for anything risky, like sending money or deleting data, require a human to approve it first. Log what the agent does so you can see why it made each choice. Guardrails are what make an agent safe to ship.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: No step limit, so it loops forever.
Running your own code as the model's tool result.
Using an agent when a workflow would do.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: no step limit, so the agent loops forever and burns money. Two: forgetting the matching tool use I D, which breaks the request. Three: confusing whose job it is to run the tool. The model asks; your code runs it and reports back. And four, the big one: reaching for an agent when a plain workflow would have been simpler, cheaper, and easier to trust. Watch for these four.

slides.title: Recap & your task
slides.narration: Let's recap. An agent runs a loop: think, act, observe, repeat. Tools give the model hands, defined by a name, a description, and an input schema. You loop until the stop reason is end turn, and you can let the S D K's tool runner handle that loop. Prefer a simple workflow when you can, and always add guardrails. Your task before the next lesson: build a tiny agent with two tools, maybe a calculator and a search stub, and watch the loop call them in turn. Great work, and I'll see you next time.
